Here, we report practical guidance for developing ideal mechanophores that promote the molecular probe’s exciton transition for room-temperature phosphorescence (RTP) under stress, through the “assisted lowest triplet (T1) state” of the adjacent polymer chain. Systematic analyses of numerous organic probes reveal that a small energy gap (ΔEM < 0.4 eV) between the probe’s lowest singlet (S1) and the polymer’s T1 states is an empirical guideline for stress-enhanced RTP. The probe-doped polymer system demonstrates not only a remarkable increase in RTP intensity of over 2000-fold upon 160 MPa but also a low stress threshold of ∼2 MPa, which is robust under 0–10 MPa cyclic pressure loading/unloading over 500 cycles. Such RTP mechanophores enable noninvasive, reversible, and molecular-level stress detection in polymers. Their doped polymers have shown potential applications in various fields for real-time sensing of stress and its uneven distribution through visual afterglow.
nb2f8f0e6ef27: Chromium-catalyzed asymmetric Nozaki–Hiyama–Kishi (NHK) reaction is a powerful tool for constructing synthetically valuable enantioenriched homoallylic alcohols and allenols. However, catalytic asymmetric NHK-type coupling of allylic or propargylic C–O electrophiles remains largely underdeveloped. Herein, we report a photomediated chromium-catalyzed deoxygenative coupling of activated allylic and propargylic alcohols with aldehydes, enabling the synthesis of a variety of chiral homoallylic alcohols with wide structural diversity and allenols. The reactions were performed under mild conditions, and a wide range of synthetically useful functional groups was found to be well tolerated. Importantly, this method provides a straightforward way for the construction of homoallylic alcohols bearing a chiral quaternary carbon center with high ee and dr. Furthermore, stereodivergent access to all four homoallylic alcohol stereoisomers is realized through orthogonal combinations of Z/E-configured allylic alcohols and R/S-configured ligands. Combined experimental and computational mechanistic studies provided insight into the key catalytic intermediate and the origin of stereocontrol.
nbaa0c04b98a5: Thiamine diphosphate (ThDP)-dependent enzymes are versatile biocatalysts for carbon–carbon bond formation, yet their catalytic repertoire has been largely confined to linear homologation and intramolecular cyclizations that rely on single-site reactive intermediates such as the Breslow or ketyl radical species. Intermolecular annulation─a powerful strategy for constructing cyclic architectures─has remained elusive within this enzyme class. Here, we report the first intermolecular [3 + 2] annulation catalyzed by a ThDP-dependent enzyme, achieved through a homoenolate-mediated nucleophilic addition pathway. A phylogeny-guided enzyme mining identified a previously uncharacterized enzyme from Variovorax boronicumulans(ThDP-5), and subsequent protein engineering yielded the F484S variant, which exhibits markedly enhanced activity and exquisite stereocontrol. This biocatalytic system exhibits a broad substrate scope (30 examples), accommodating diverse substituted cinnamaldehydes and isatins to afford chiral spirooxindole lactones with excellent stereoselectivity (up to > 20:1 dr and 99% ee). Preparative-scale reactions (2 mmol) validate its synthetic utility. This work expands ThDP-dependent biocatalysis to intermolecular annulations, providing a robust and selective platform for the construction of pharmaceutically relevant spirocyclic architectures.
n333afcc79cbb: Many O2-activating mononuclear nonheme iron enzymes require substrate or cofactor/cosubstrate coordination to iron to form the key peroxy-bridged intermediate necessary for catalysis with no net change in the iron redox state. The role of (co)substrate coordination, however, remained unclear. Here, we leverage a pterin-dependent enzyme, tryptophan hydroxylase, for which cosubstrate (pterin) coordination can be experimentally controlled by the absence and presence of substrate, to explicitly determine the role of pterin coordination in O2 binding and peroxo formation. EPR, absorption, circular dichroism, and magnetic circular dichroism spectroscopies on the {FeNO}7 analog of the unobservable {FeO2}8 intermediate without and with pterin coordination demonstrate that pterin coordination induces new absorption bands and enhances NO affinity by 3.6 kcal mol–1 at 277 K. These new bands are pterin-to-iron ligand-to-metal charge-transfer transitions that compensate the electron donation from iron to NO upon NO binding. Extension of our findings on {FeNO}7 to {FeO2}8 evidences that pterin coordination stabilizes O2 binding and facilitates the two-electron transfer from pterin to {FeO2}8 to reduce the transition-state barrier for peroxo formation by 12.7 kcal mol–1, corresponding to a 1010 increase in reaction rate. The electron transfer pathways established herein underscore a unified mechanism for the pterin-dependent, α-ketoglutarate-dependent, extradiol, and intradiol dioxygenase families of mononuclear nonheme iron enzymes through which (co)substrate coordination enhances O2 binding via one-electron transfer within {FeO2}8 and two-electron donation from the (co)substrate (one to bound O2 and one to iron) to generate the peroxo species with no net redox change on the iron.
nf6fdf601de3e: The search for selective anion receptors that can function in water is a longstanding challenge in supramolecular chemistry, motivated by anions’ fundamental roles (and potential applications) in biological, environmental, and industrial processes. Here, we incorporate halogen and hydrogen bond donors into an easy-to-prepare organic cage molecule and demonstrate that this can bind anions at either or both of a halogen-bonding pocket and hydrogen-bonding pockets depending on the nature of the anions and the solvent. The halogen-bonding pocket comprising six bromopyridinium donors is a potent host for iodide anions and can selectively bind this guest in water as strongly as biological iodide binders (Ka = 43,000 M–1 measured by 1H NMR spectroscopy) with the exclusion of other halide anions. In DMSO/water mixtures, the hydrogen-bonding pockets are able to recognize chloride anions, resulting in the formation of mixed anion iodide/chloride complexes with an iodide bound in the center of the cage and chlorides in the peripheral binding sites. This demonstrates the exquisite selectivity afforded by halogen-bonding systems and reveals a general route to a range of supramolecular anion hosts that bind multiple guests in different locations.
nc9be3d6fe0ad: Widespread deployment of sodium-ion batteries demands both high energy density and reliable low-temperature (LT) operation, but is constrained by a persistent trade-off between high-voltage stability (cathode/electrolyte) and LT ion-transport kinetics. Herein, we report a solvent/anion codepleted solvation engineering strategy to construct low-coordination electrolytes through competitive anion complexation mediated by a bulky electron-deficient additive, TMSB (tris(trimethylsilyl)borate). We reveal that TMSB preferentially complexes with PF6– to suppress direct anion-Na+ coordination, while its bulky steric backbone disrupts conventional ion-pair networks and restricts excessive solvent-Na+ coordination. This strategy fundamentally boosts ionic conductivity (from 2.41 to 5.34 mS cm–1) and lowers the desolvation energy barrier (from 44.82 to 33.97 kJ mol–1). Moreover, such a strategy enables a high-modulus (2.7 GPa), inorganic-rich cathode-electrolyte interphase (CEI), which can not only mitigate surface degradation, but also suppress bulk phase transitions of cathode materials. Consequently, the electrolyte demonstrates broad compatibility across diverse cathodes (NFM, NVP, and P2-NNMO) under extreme voltage (up to 4.5 V) and temperature (−40 to 25 °C) conditions. Remarkably, the scaled-up 6.8 Ah pouch cell achieves a record-high energy density of 200 Wh kg–1 at 25 °C, while maintaining 162 Wh kg–1 even at −20 °C, offering a generalizable molecular paradigm for extreme-environment energy storage.
n6938f8ce713a: Intracellular protein condensates formed by liquid–liquid phase separation have gained increasing attention in recent years due to their key roles in many physiological and pathological processes. However, fluorescence imaging of protein condensates is limited by the bulky fluorescent tags that could perturb the protein localization and interaction. Imaging techniques that can visualize protein condensates in live cells with minimal perturbations remain lacking. Here, we develop a strategy to image intracellular protein condensates by coupling stimulated Raman scattering (SRS) microscopy to specific amino acid labeling. Different types of amino acids are found to exhibit distinct incorporation patterns in the live cells. By metabolic labeling of deuterated tyrosine-d4 and arginine-d7, ALS-related fused in sarcoma (FUS) protein condensates can be visualized with a high specificity. In addition, two-color pulse-chase imaging reveals protein translation arrest in FUS condensates under stress conditions. Furthermore, heterogeneous tyrosine phosphorylation is imaged in live cells and FUS condensates based on the Raman blue shift of phosphorylated tyrosine-d4. Thus, our technique to image specific amino acids by SRS provides a new platform to visualize the metabolic turnover and post-translational modifications of protein condensates in live cells with minimal perturbation.
n875be8dbb9ab: Molecular solar thermal (MOST) energy storage compounds capture solar photon energy in the strained chemical bonds of metastable photoisomers and release it on demand as heat, yet simultaneously achieving visible-light absorption and high energy storage density has remained a persistent challenge. Here we introduce 9-aryl acridine N-oxides as MOST compounds based on visible-light-driven dearomative ring expansion. Irradiation at 470 nm, near the solar irradiance maximum at 482 nm, quantitatively converts these compounds to metastable 1,2-oxazepines, which thermally revert to the parent N-oxides and discharge the stored energy. The system achieves energy storage densities of up to 0.54 MJ/kg, comparable to Dewar anthracenes, while absorbing substantially more red-shifted light and offering nearly 3 orders of magnitude longer storage lifetimes of up to 1.4 years in the solid state. The thermal half-lives of the 1,2-oxazepines are tunable through para-substitution on the aryl ring and solvation, enabling up to a 1,300-fold reduction in half-life. Crucially, the 9-aryl substituent biases the transient oxaziridine intermediate toward selective reversion to the N-oxide over competing decomposition pathways, overcoming the limitations of other acridine N-oxides reported to date. This work establishes light-induced ring expansion as an effective strategy for MOST and expands the scope of viable MOST compounds.
n7230f04c0938: Mechanocatalysis harnesses ubiquitous mechanical energy for sustainable chemical transformations, but its development is hindered by conceptual fragmentation. This review proposes a process-oriented framework, deconstructing mechanocatalysis into four sequential stages: energy coupling, transduction, charge transport, and electronic behavior. This framework provides a mechanistic basis for the rational design of mechanocatalytic systems, paving the way for standardized evaluation and broader applications.
nb4515d30671f: Modern electronics require polymer composites that integrate electromagnetic wave absorption (EWA) and thermal dissipation, yet these functions impose competing structural requirements. Herein, we construct Fe single-atom@short-range graphitized porous carbon (Fe1@SGC) that integrates electromagnetic attenuation and thermal conduction within a single material. Distinct from conventional exogenous metal-introduction routes, egg white serves as both the carbon source and coordination medium, enabling Fe single-atom anchoring without metal salts or organic ligands. Fe single atoms induce charge redistribution, polarization centers, and local ordering of carbon domains, synergistically regulating dielectric loss, thermal transport, and impedance matching. The multiscale carbon network further promotes electromagnetic wave penetration and multiple reflections/scattering. After incorporation into polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), the Fe1@SGC/PTFE composite achieves a maximum effective absorption bandwidth of 7.92 GHz and improved thermal conductivity. This work establishes endogenous single-atom-induced local graphitization as a ligand-free and structurally precise strategy for designing single-component fillers toward integrated EWA and thermal management.
n52bf7f2aca3f: Solution-processed thin films of colloidal lead halide perovskite (LHP) nanocrystals (NCs) show great potential for next-generation optoelectronic devices. However, these NC solids exhibit non-negligible size and shape polydispersity, which introduces both structural and energetic disorder. Here we resolve the exciton dynamics in space, time, and energy to elucidate the impact of disorder on exciton transport. We show that the disorder depends sensitively on the alkylamine ligand used in the synthesis. While shorter alkyl chain lengths lead to high polydispersity, longer alkyl chains lead to a narrower size distribution and smaller particles where quantum confinement becomes more pronounced, consequently leading to increased energetic disorder. Strikingly, we find that exciton transport is less efficient in NC solids with long alkyl chains, despite the fact that they have significantly more narrowly size-distributed ensembles. This demonstrates that energetic disorder rather than structural disorder is the dominant factor for predicting exciton transport within these disordered systems.
n9477007182f2: Organic electrochemical transistors (OECTs) are promising building blocks for flexible in-sensor computing, yet the conflicting ionic dynamic demands of high-fidelity sensing and nonvolatile memory remain challenging to reconcile within a unified hardware platform. Here, we report a hierarchical compositional programming strategy that addresses this trade-off across a standardized stretchable OECT architecture. Regulating 2,2,6,6-tetramethylpiperidine-1-oxyl (TEMPO)-oxidized cellulose nanofiber content in poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene) (PEDOT) tunes channel capacitance and mechanical compliance, while tailoring the supramolecular network in a deep eutectic solvent gel electrolyte dictates ion retention kinetics. This strategy establishes distinct operational regimes via tailored formulations: a rapidly reversible, low-hysteresis state for sensing and a persistent ion trapping state for neuromorphic computing. The sensing OECT enables real-time electrocardiogram acquisition with a 35.6 dB signal-to-noise ratio and 98.9% biometric identification accuracy across 15 subjects. The computing state supports temporal Morse code demodulation and Pavlovian associative learning, demonstrating application-adaptive stretchable bioelectronics.
n15da774e9381: Probing anisotropic electron–phonon interactions (EPIs) is fundamental to understanding low-dimensional quantum materials, yet isolating their intrinsic signatures remains a challenge due to the confounding influence of extrinsic effects. Here, we resolve this ambiguity in quasi-one-dimensional Ta2Ni3Te5 through a combination of angle-resolved polarized Raman spectroscopy and density functional perturbation theory (DFPT). Anomalous four-lobe angular dependences were observed in Ag phonon modes, which deviate from the real-valued Raman tensor prediction. Further, we explicitly highlight that, despite their distinct physical origins, light absorption and birefringence yield mathematically identical angular dependencies in Ta2Ni3Te5, rendering phenomenological fitting alone insufficient to identify the true physical mechanism. By employing a full quantum treatment incorporating detailed interaction mechanisms, we capture the qualitative characteristics and mode-to-mode diversity of the anomalous angular responses observed experimentally. The DFPT calculations further reveal mode-specific and momentum-resolved EPIs, providing microscopic support for anisotropic EPIs as the mechanism of anomalous Raman responses.
n38a4560d2e4b: The conductivity-swelling trade-off limits anion exchange membranes (AEMs) for water electrolysis. Here, we investigated how the timing of tetraphenylmethane (TPM) incorporation influences precursor assembly and membrane hydration in poly(aryl piperidinium) AEMs. Introducing TPM before backbone extension alters precursor formation and favors a more uniform distribution of hydrophilic domains in the resulting membranes. Spectroscopic and NMR analyses further associate this route with enhanced hydrogen-bond organization and increased local mobility within the hydrated membranes. The optimized P-TPM5 membrane reaches an OH– conductivity of 229.4 ± 6 mS cm–1 at 80 °C while maintaining a swelling ratio of approximately 15%. In an AEM water electrolyzer containing a NiFe-LDH anode and Pt/C cathode, the membrane delivers 5.74 A cm–2 at 2.0 V and operates for more than 1100 h in a staged-current test. These results identify the timing of branching-unit incorporation as a synthesis variable for tailoring hydration environments and improving the conductivity-swelling balance of AEMs.
nbe25b754b84e: Antimicrobial polymers offer an attractive tool for combating the crisis of antimicrobial resistance. This Review highlights recent advances in antimicrobial polymer development and discusses future directions, including the use of machine learning to guide polymer design and the development of scalable production methods to ensure global accessibility of these materials.
na1605d9f2801: Single-atom catalysts can mitigate reliance on scarce noble metals, but isolated sites can be fragile. Here a catalyst with proximal Ru−O−Cr motifs is fabricated that demonstrates proximal oxidation damping where the Cr neighbour buffers Ru overoxidation, improving stability for acidic oxygen evolution.
ncf8e4c0467cb: Nitroalkanes are widely used as nucleophiles via their nitronate ions to construct carbon skeletons before the nitro group is transformed. Their use as electrophiles, however, is limited by the poor leaving group ability of the nitro group and competing α-deprotonation. Conventional substitution has also been severely constrained by the structural requirements for stabilizing reactive intermediates. Photocatalytic denitrative cyanation was developed to allow substitution in nonactivated secondary nitroalkanes.
n458c3fc53607: Hyaluronic acid (HA) is a major glycosaminoglycan of the vertebrate extracellular matrix whose biological functions depend strongly on its molecular weight. Controlled depolymerization of HA into defined oligosaccharides is therefore of considerable biomedical and biotechnological interest. Although bacterial HA lyases have been extensively characterized, fungal HA-degrading enzymes remain poorly understood, and none has been structurally assigned to a defined CAZy family. Here, we identify and characterize PlLya44, an HA lyase secreted by the filamentous fungus Purpureocillium lilacinum. The enzyme was detected in the fungal secretome, produced in Pichia pastoris, and shown to efficiently depolymerize high molecular weight HA, generating mainly unsaturated oligosaccharides with both even- and odd-numbered products. Product analysis supports a predominantly processive endolytic mode of action distinct from the classical exo-processive mechanism of bacterial HA lyases. The crystal structure of PlLya44 uncovers an α-helical α6/α6 barrel fold characteristic of the (α/α)n toroid superfamily, harboring an elongated polarity-partitioned catalytic cleft. Structural comparisons and sequence similarity network analyses demonstrate that PlLya44 does not cluster with any currently defined polysaccharide lyase (PL) family, supporting its classification as the founding member of a distinct PL family. Ligand-bound structures, mutagenesis, ensemble refinement, and molecular dynamics reveal a reorganized catalytic architecture, reversing substrate orientation relative to previously characterized HA lyases. Together, these findings provide structural insight into a fungal HA lyase, uncover a previously unrecognized catalytic strategy for HA depolymerization, and establish PlLya44 as the founding member of a hitherto undescribed PL family, expanding the enzymatic landscape of glycosaminoglycan-active enzymes.
nfc212e0a074e: Precise photocatalytic modulation of the NAD+/NADH redox balance is critical for advancing both biocatalytic cascade reactions and photodynamic therapy, yet this goal remains elusive due to the scarcity of efficient, broad-spectrum photocatalysts with orthogonal redox regulation capabilities. Herein, we report a bifunctional covalent organic framework-polyoxometalate (COF-POM) composite that enables bidirectional photocatalytic interconversion between NAD+ and NADH under red visible light irradiation, achieving 77.0% yield for NADH regeneration and nearly quantitative conversion in NADH oxidation. Strikingly, cyt c-mediated anaerobic NADH oxidation was successfully realized, enabling spatiotemporally precise modulation of the intracellular NAD+/NADH redox balance. Mechanistic investigations reveal that POM integration synergistically reinforces the built-in electric field of the COF matrix, substantially accelerating photogenerated charge separation and interfacial transfer kinetics. This work establishes a generalizable strategy for constructing high-performance photocatalysts to enable precise NAD+/NADH redox balance regulation for future tumor metabolic intervention.
n44bb79c94dec: This study investigates the durability of α-MnO2, one of the most cost-effective catalysts for the oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) in alkaline media. A comprehensive set of various characterization techniques, including identical location transmission electron microscopy (IL-TEM), differential electrochemical mass spectrometry (DEMS), rotating ring-disk electrode (RRDE), and online inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) coupled to both flow cell and gas diffusion electrode (GDE) half-cell, was employed. In addition, accelerated stress test (AST) measurements in the GDE half-cell followed by post mortem X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), synchrotron X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and TEM analysis were performed. Three electrolyte and temperature combinations ranging from standard lab conditions to application-relevant conditions were systematically investigated. The results reveal that Mn dissolution occurs under oxygen-free conditions due to oxidation-state transitions of the catalyst, whereas under oxygen, it is further accelerated by degradation processes associated with peroxide formation as a byproduct of the ORR, particularly at higher ORR overpotentials. Both increasing KOH concentration and temperature significantly enhance Mn dissolution due to accelerated Mn reduction and dissolution kinetics. Despite the increased dissolution, the condition of 4.0 M KOH at 25 °C exhibits the highest ORR activity after 5000 AST cycles. This apparent discrepancy is attributed to surface roughening of the catalyst, leading to an increased electrochemically active surface area. Overall, the results demonstrate that α-MnO2 exhibits promising initial ORR activity but undergoes substantial Mn dissolution under operating conditions. These findings provide mitigation strategies to limit catalyst degradation and improve operational durability.
n826c0e7f2563: Microbial N–C bond cleavage plays a vital role in the nitrogen biogeochemical cycle. Heme-dependent oxidative N-demethylase (HODM), an enzyme identified within the Per-ARNT-Sim (PAS) domain family, challenges the traditional view of PAS domains as merely sensory modules by catalyzing the dimethylamine (DMA) demethylation to methylamine (MA) and formaldehyde via N–C bond dissociation. In this study, we employed density functional calculations to investigate the mechanistic landscape of the HODM reaction across multiple spin states. Among nine mechanistic pathways examined, two (mechanisms A1 and A3) proceeding on the doublet-state surface were found to be viable, mainly involving (1) addition of an electron to the enzyme-substrate complex generating Fe(III)–O22– anion, (2) proton transfer from Arg224 forming Fe(III)––OOH (Cpd 0), (3) homolytic O─O bond cleavage producing heme high-valent O═Fe(IV)(Por) (Cpd II) and •OH radical, (4) hydrogen-atom transfer (HAT) from DMA to •OH yielding water, and (5) second HAT from DMA to Cpd II producing imine that hydrolyzes nonenzymatically to MA and formaldehyde. The DMA hydrogen abstraction by •OH is rate-limiting. Our findings establish HODM as an amine oxidase with •OH as the initial active species to abstract substrate hydrogens, instead of a monooxygenase using high-valent iron(IV)–oxo. Cpd 0 could not work as the H-abstraction species. Without an electron gained, the Fe(III)–O2•– superoxide radical is unable to initiate the HODM reaction. The revelation of HODM nature expands the PAS chemistry and enriches the understanding of enzymatic N–C bond dissociation and heme chemistry.
n6d5bcd2455a0: Olefins production from syngas via Fischer–Tropsch synthesis requires catalysts that favor olefins formation, maintain intrinsic activity, and suppress CO2 and CH4 formation. Sodium-promoted ruthenium nanoparticles shift the product distribution toward α-olefins but suppress Ru activity by more than 90%, necessitating higher Ru loadings. We show that incorporating inorganic fluorine into Na-promoted Ru catalysts increases activity 2.5-fold while maintaining 72.1% α-olefins selectivity and ∼5.0% combined selectivity to CO2 and CH4. At a Ru loading of 1.26 wt %, the catalyst achieves a Ru time yield of 1.14 molCO·gRu–1·h–1 and olefins space-time yield of 1516.1 g·molRu–1·h–1, outperforming most reported Ru-based catalysts. Fluorine also restores activity in Fe- and Co-based systems. Mechanistic studies indicate that surface Na–F cation–anion pairs modulate the electronic structure, weaken Ru-CO binding, and generate hydrogen species that accelerate CO activation and suppress olefins hydrogenation. This work established a halogen-mediated strategy to address the activity–selectivity trade-off in sodium-promoted syngas conversion.
ncaa7ff6f0eea: Emerging machine learning (ML) approaches offer transformative strategies to accelerate discovery for challenging objectives, such as developing practical catalysts through rational design. We propose an iterative learning framework and strategy that effectively enhances the predictive capability of the ML model, thereby accelerating catalyst development. By leveraging low-performance catalytic results, we have proven a practical, scalable framework for data-efficient catalyst development and for the broader application of ML methods in heterogeneous catalysis. The ML approach effectively captures the intrinsic relationship between metal type/content and catalytic performance, thereby enhancing prediction accuracy through iterative optimization. The case example regards the development of metal-supported catalysts for CO2 reduction. The results show that incorporating low-performance catalytic results into the iterative learning process markedly improves the predictive accuracy of the random forest (RF) model (R2 increased from 0.80 to 0.86, and mean square error (RMSE) decreased from 1.20% to 0.89%). The deviations between the experimental and predicted values for the CO2 reduction performance of the four catalysts identified through this approach were all less than 2%, demonstrating the model's reliability and predictive capability. Among them, the 1.5Pt2Fe/TiO2-R catalyst exhibited high CO2 reduction activity and long-term stability (>200 h), highlighting the practical potential of ML-guided catalyst design. The use of low-performance catalytic data outperforms high-performance ones in improving predictive accuracy when coupled with a suitable iterative learning framework, providing mechanistic insight into how they help the model define the boundaries of the feasible performance region.
n70fb9b976d0f: Electrochemical H2O2 synthesis via the two-electron oxygen reduction reaction (2e– ORR) enables on-site production, yet its practical application is hindered by the scarcity of catalysts that can simultaneously deliver high selectivity, activity, and stability at industrial current densities. Here, we report molybdenum incorporation into nickel oxide, where Mo is predominantly present as atomically dispersed, oxygen-coordinated Mo species (denoted as MoOx). The resulting MoOx–NiO catalyst features a hybrid crystalline–amorphous structure. Spectroscopy and density functional theory calculations reveal that MoOx induces a localized electron redistribution, generating electron-rich Ni sites with a formal valence below + 2 (Ni2–x) adjacent to MoOx as key active sites. These Ni2–x sites tune the adsorption free energy of the critical OOH intermediate and favor the 2e– pathway over the competing 4e– pathway. The MoOx–NiO achieves >95% H2O2 selectivity over a potential range of 0.25–0.70 V vs RHE and a high production rate of 34.8 ± 0.8 mol gcat–1 h–1 at an industrial current density of 200 mA cm–2 in a flow cell, together with high Faradic efficiency and long-term operational stability. These findings show that engineering the chemical state and oxygen coordination of a dopant can modulate the local electronic structures of host metal sites and thereby influence catalytic pathways, providing a strategy for the design of advanced oxide electrocatalysts.
n62f6a3dd1b4b: Non-thermal plasma (NTP) catalysis enables the direct co-conversion of CH4 and CO2 into thermodynamically limited liquid products under mild conditions. However, achieving high selectivity toward liquid products and clarifying the role of the catalyst in steering product distribution remain significant challenges. Here we uncover a previously unrecognized mechanism governing selectivity in plasma catalysis: the formation of a reservoir of strongly adsorbed surface species that evolves during reaction and dynamically controls liquid-product formation. We investigated the catalytic performance, catalyst structure, plasma properties, and surface species during time-dependent liquid methanol production—in addition to valuable syngas and C2 hydrocarbons in the gas stream—over an α-Fe2O3 catalyst. Stable catalyst structure and plasma conditions were unable to explain the transient product selectivity towards methanol. Instead, in situ plasma–IR studies revealed that strongly bound C═O and C–H species progressively accumulated with time-on-stream (TOS) and correlated with the observed increase in methanol yield. The strongly bound C═O and C–H species are proposed to enhance methanol selectivity by modifying the surface Brønsted and Lewis acidity, promoting methoxy hydrogenation, and weakening methanol adsorption. Studying the plasma interaction of select reaction species (CH4, CO2, CO, methanol, acetaldehyde, and acetic acid) with the catalyst surface showed that the main liquid product, methanol, was responsible for populating the surface with hydrogenated carbonyl species that boosted its own production. A methanol-plasma pretreatment was envisioned and implemented to preload a reservoir of the C═O and C–H species on the surface of α-Fe2O3, resulting in a significant improvement in catalyst performance for selective methanol production. After 8 h TOS, the treated catalyst exhibited a 30% relative increase in selectivity and a threefold increase in methanol yield compared to the untreated catalyst, offering a promising route toward highly selective liquid product formation. Additionally, the methanol–plasma pretreatment to boost methanol production was extended to other metal oxide catalysts, highlighting the broad versatility and potential of this strategy across a wide range of plasma catalyst systems.
n9613e6e2b8eb: Oxygen species evolution is central to the catalytic performance of oxidative coupling of methane (OCM), yet understanding and controlling this evolution remains a major challenge. SrTiO3 is a promising OCM catalyst due to its high C2 selectivity and stability but suffers from low activity. Here, DFT calculations combined with kMC simulations were employed to investigate facet-dependent oxygen species cycling on SrTiO3. Our findings reveal that SrTiO3(100)-Ti is the most favorable facet, sustaining a regenerable oxygen cycle (“O2− → OV → O22− → Ti-OH → O2−”). The local oxygen chemical potential (μO) is further identified as a thermodynamic descriptor linking oxygen stability with CH4* activation ability, following the order OV > O22− > Ti-OH > O2−. Furthermore, the spatial distribution of OV acts as a structural switch, directing two competing Mars–van Krevelen (MvK) cycles. kMC simulations reveal that the peroxide-mediated pathway dominates under operando conditions, whereas the overall activity is limited by the low activity of O2− and the accumulation of inert OlatH that further poisons active sites. Notably, B-site La doping effectively overcomes this bottleneck by activating OlatH and increasing the μO of O2− from –9.12 eV to –6.57 eV, which enhances the CH4(g) turnover frequency from 4.79 × 10−1 to 2.40 s−1 at 1073.15 K. These results establish μO and oxygen vacancy distribution as general design principles for perovskite oxide catalysts, offering a promising strategy to enhance OCM activity.
n3d7acf6de384: Pulsed electrochemical CO2 reduction on Cu catalysts represents a promising strategy to mitigate catalyst degradation and sustain high selectivity toward multicarbon (C2+) products. However, developing a detailed mechanistic understanding of the oxidative pulses remains challenging due to the inability to resolve the Cu oxidation state and the local electrolyte pH in the vicinity of the catalyst, especially inside a porous gas diffusion electrode. In this study, we investigate the impact of different potential pulse profiles on the recovery of CO and C2+ product selectivity, the latter representing C–C coupling. The potential-pH trajectories of the pulses are mapped onto calculated potential-pH Cu phase diagrams for CO2-saturated aqueous KCl and KHCO3 electrolytes to identify the thermodynamically accessible Cu phases during pulses. We show that abrupt pulses at a local alkaline pH lead to simultaneous C2+ and CO recovery. In contrast, quasi-adiabatic pulses, where the local pH remains equilibrated with the bulk pH, recover CO selectivity independently of C2+ products. Furthermore, in acidic KCl electrolytes, where no Cu oxide is thermodynamically accessible during a quasi-adiabatic pulse, the recovery of C2+ is attributed to Cu dissolution and redeposition. Importantly, this finding demonstrates that the formation of a Cu oxide phase, even temporarily during the pulse, is not required for C–C coupling. In contrast, in KHCO3 electrolyte, the formation of a Cu oxide phase remains thermodynamically accessible during pulses. Moreover, we show that the oxidative charge of the pulse recovering CO selectivity scales with prior reduction time, hypothesized to be a removal of surface poisoning species. Our findings enable rational design of pulse protocols based on electrolyte-, potential-, and pH-resolved Cu phase diagrams and provide a framework that can be extended to other catalysts and electrolytes.
nc174700223a6: The direct synthesis of ethanol from syngas faces a key challenge: achieving high selectivity at high CO conversion while elucidating the catalytic reaction mechanism. Here, we develop a catalyst comprising highly dispersed Rh–Fe bimetallic nano-islands supported on mixed-phase TiO2, which overcomes the trade-off between catalytic activity and ethanol selectivity, achieving an ethanol selectivity of 62.5% among all carbon-containing products at a CO conversion of 55.8%. Meanwhile, CO2 selectivity is greatly reduced to 8.1%. Mechanistic studies reveal that the breakthrough stems from the enhanced density of interfacial active sites, that the Fe species modulate the local electronic environment to optimize the Rhδ+/Rh0 ratio, and Rhδ+ species in contact with the TiO2 support are stably anchored via the formation of FeOx–Rhδ+–Ov–Ti3+ interfacial sites. The in situ diffuse reflectance infrared Fourier transform spectroscopy (DRIFTS), chemical transient kinetics (CTK), and density functional theory (DFT) characterizations reveal that the surface Rh0 sites facilitate CO dissociation and hydrogenation, whereas the FeOx–Rhδ+–Ov–Ti3+ interfacial sites promote the coupling of CHx with CHxO while suppressing the CO* + O → CO2 pathway. This work provides a route for suppressing CO2 formation and enhancing ethanol production in syngas conversion.
nc7c144f49cd7: Long-term failure of resin–dentin bonding arises from persistent hydration and enzymatic degradation of exposed collagen in the deep hybrid layer, whereas diffusion of bioactive components through dentinal tubules toward the pulp may cause pulpal irritation. An ideal pretreatment should therefore promote collagen remineralization and interfacial stabilization while reducing pulp-adjacent cellular irritation and supporting pulp–dentin repair. Herein, supramolecular complexes of chlorogenic acid (CGA) and cucurbit[n]uril (Q[n], n = 6, 7, and 8), denoted CGA@Q[n], were constructed to regulate CGA loading, release, and interfacial exposure. CGA@Q[6] showed limited loading, release, and mineralization capacity. CGA@Q[7] exhibited faster early release and achieved complete collagen mineralization within 24 h, whereas CGA@Q[8] showed the highest encapsulation efficiency, sustained CGA supply, complete mineralization at 36 h, and a continuous, dense, integrated intrafibrillar mineral phase. Molecular dynamics simulations indicated that CGA released from Q[8] reanchored to collagen and recruited Ca2+, promoting mineral formation within confined intrafibrillar spaces. These advantages extended to three-dimensional collagen networks and demineralized dentin, yielding higher HAp content, enhanced mineral–collagen integration, tubule occlusion, mechanical recovery, and MMP-9 inhibition. As a bonding pretreatment, CGA@Q[8] reduced nanoleakage, endogenous gelatinolytic activity, and aging-induced bond-strength loss. It also improved cytocompatibility relative to free CGA and promoted mineralization and odontogenic differentiation of human dental pulp stem cells (hDPSCs). In vivo, CGA@Q[8] promoted dentin remineralization, maintained near-pulp interfacial stability, alleviated pulpal irritation, and enhanced odontogenic repair. Together, these findings identify CGA@Q[8] as the most effective formulation and show that homologue selection can tune CGA exposure kinetics for coordinated dentin interface repair.
n93957f5a17b2: Cu hydride nanoclusters with atomic precision in composition and structure offer exciting catalytic activities and opportunities for rigorous structure–function correlations. Determination of their atomic structures, especially the hydride locations, hinges on the availability of high-quality single crystals and neutron beams, while their relatively weak UV–visible absorption and electrochemical instability challenge the analysis of their electronic properties. Herein, we synthesize a Cu14H10 nanocluster coordinated by three 4-mercaptobenzonitrile (MBN) and eight triphenylphosphine ligands. Two-dimensional NMR analyses combined with single crystal X-ray diffraction reveal unequivocally the locations of the ten hydrides in four groups (stoichiometry ratio of 1:3:3:3) with drastically different environments (chemical shifts 11–3 ppm): one H at the inversion center and three triangular layers along the C3 axial bridging together the Cu core. MBN serves two additional purposes besides stabilizing ligands: its electron-withdrawing nature and a highly sensitive vibrational reporter of its local charge density. The first property gives rise to a low-lying Cu-core-to-MBN metal-to-ligand charge transfer (MLCT) excited state, and the second property enables direct spectroscopic probing of both the charge transfer nature and dynamics of the MLCT excited state through the dynamic spectral shift of the MBN CN stretching mode. Through combined transient IR absorption spectroscopy and time-dependent density functional theory (TD-DFT) calculations, we obtained the complete atomic and electronic structure, revealing core-to-ligand charge transfers in these nanoclusters. Computed under identical conditions using an iso-structure with a mildly electron-donating ligand, the Cu14H10 featuring charge delocalization toward the electron-withdrawing MBN has a smaller HOMO–LUMO gap, which is deemed favorable for electrocatalytic CO2 reduction. The preferential formation of complex multielectron-hydrogenation products (8–12 e–, C1 hydrocarbons, and C2+ products) over two-electron pathways such as CO formation or the competing hydrogen evolution reaction highlights their promise as atomically precise catalysts for deep CO2 reduction.
n31f149fdad99: Carbon nanotubes (CNTs) combine high electrical conductivity, mechanical robustness, and nanoscale architecture, making them promising materials for neural interfaces. However, the strong coupling between CNT morphology, electrical transport, and surface chemistry has limited identification of the material properties that directly regulate neuronal function. Here, we establish an experimental strategy to disentangle morphology-dependent network transport from interfacial wettability using pristine-like CNT coatings. Multiwalled CNTs with comparable diameters but distinct lengths were reversibly functionalized, spray-coated, and thermally defunctionalized to produce homogeneous conductive networks while recovering pristine-like electrical transport and surface chemistry. Subsequent conditioning in phosphate-buffered saline substantially reduced surface hydrophobicity without detectable alteration of the graphitic CNT framework, generating coatings with comparable interfacial wettability but distinct network morphologies. Primary spinal cord neuron-glia cultures grown on these substrates were characterized by immunocytochemistry, electrophysiology, and calcium imaging. All CNT coatings supported comparable neuroglial density and network formation, whereas PBS-conditioned coatings, characterized by a more wettable interface, consistently exhibited enhanced spontaneous bursting and calcium activity compared with their untreated coatings. Across all conditions, neuronal network activity was more consistently associated with the initial interfacial state of CNT coatings, as experimentally reflected by their wetting behavior, than with CNT length or morphology-dependent electrical transport. These findings identify the initial CNT interfacial state, with wettability serving as an experimentally accessible descriptor, as a key design parameter for CNT-based neural interfaces. Furthermore, they suggest that the initial interfacial state may influence the subsequent evolution of the biomolecular layer at the cell-facing interface, thereby contributing to the modulation of neuronal function.
n3d3827ca855c: Preserving exciton delocalization in the presence of structural and environmental disorder is a central challenge for nanoscale photonic and optoelectronic materials. Here we show that Frenkel excitons in two-dimensional supramolecular nanostructures retain extensive delocalization even in the presence of intentionally incorporated deep-energy traps. Fluorescent trap molecules introduced during the self-assembly of double-walled molecular nanotubes provide a controlled model system in which strong local energetic perturbations are created without significant distortion of the host structure. Increasing the trap concentration shortens the host-exciton PL lifetime from ∼190 ps to ∼15 ps, while polarization-resolved microscopy of individual nanotubes shows that the collective excitonic polarization remains essentially unchanged. Frenkel-exciton calculations based on experimentally established molecular structures reproduce this robustness and reveal that delocalization decreases only weakly because the excitonic wave functions redistribute around the trap sites while remaining extended over large molecular domains. These results demonstrate an intrinsic defect tolerance of delocalized Frenkel excitons in a two-dimensional supramolecular architecture and identify dimensionality as an important design principle for preserving collective excitonic states in structurally imperfect nanomaterials.
nabfe3e2579e5: Bone infection is a common and serious complication in orthopedic surgery. Conventional antibiotic strategies frequently induce antibiotic resistance, leading to the persistence of bone infections. In this study, an engineered peptide nanoparticle named C8-IK21 was designed based on the coiled-coil motif. Specifically, C8-IK21 effectively targeted bacterial cell membranes, further exacerbating bacterial death through lipid peroxidation. At safe doses, local administration of C8-IK21 demonstrated high efficacy in treating S. aureus-infected cortical bone defects in mice. No detectable resistance emerged under the tested experimental conditions. Additionally, C8-IK21 exhibited anti-inflammatory activity. Furthermore, C8-IK21 could enter cells by binding to ADAM9, activating the ERK signaling pathway to regulate osteoblast differentiation. Meanwhile, C8-IK21 reduced the expression of ITGB1 via ADAM9, thereby inhibiting osteoclast differentiation and function. Moreover, the pro-osteogenic effect of C8-IK21 was validated in organoids. In conclusion, C8-IK21 represents a promising therapeutic approach for the treatment of refractory bacterial infections and bone homeostasis disorders.
n5e05be565909: Miniaturized spectrometers are essential for portable and consumer-oriented applications, yet their reduced physical footprint inherently limits the detector’s active area, leading to compromised sensitivity. Conventional strategies to enhance sensitivity, such as cryogenic cooling or photomultiplier tubes, are incompatible with miniaturization due to their bulk, cost, and power demands. Here, we present a miniaturized spectrometer based on a van der Waals heterojunction integrated on a ferroelectric thin film. Spectral discrimination is enabled by engineering both interlayer and intralayer photoresponses within the heterojunction, which can be dynamically tuned solely via the source-drain bias, eliminating the need for a gate electrode and enabling a two-terminal architecture. This design is inherently compatible with simple two-pad readout integrated circuits, facilitating scalable array integration for compact spectroscopic systems. Critically, the built-in electric field generated by the ferroelectric polarization promotes efficient dissociation of interlayer excitons, yielding an ultralow noise floor of below 5 × 10–16 A Hz–1/2, more than 2 orders of magnitude lower than existing miniaturized spectrometers and surpassing the performance of most benchtop instruments. This work in sensitivity without sacrificing size or complexity present a strategy for deploying high-performance spectroscopy in real-world applications.
na82c156821eb: Nanopore sequencing for full-length proteins is daunting due to inaccuracy of fingerprinting amino acids with ionic current and lack of theoretical models. Here, we demonstrate that nanopores drilled in 5 nm-thick membranes with constriction diameter <1 nm, i.e., subnanopores, can site-specifically read the primary structure of amyloid-β (Aβ) isoforms after 50-fold coverage. Molecular dynamics simulations reveal that charged side chains near the constriction swing and modulate the volume exclusion of neighboring residues, resulting in a sequence context-dependent signal altered between translocation orientations. Orientation of individual label-free molecules is inferred by clustering, which yields high-fidelity empirical consensus that strongly correlates with computational trajectories (PCC = 0.78 ± 0.03). A homemade self-supervised learning method categorizes Aβ42 and Aβ40 at the single-molecule level (AUC = 0.88 ± 0.02) and predicts the mole fraction in agreement with actual ratios. Solid-state subnanopores offer a straightforward strategy for proteoform single-molecule classification and sequence extraction in mixtures.
nd9bcaf1faf53: The treatment of infectious diabetic wound is greatly hampered by hyperglycemia, inflammation, and microcirculatory dysfunction. Bioelectric stimulation and nanozyme catalysis provide a potential strategy for chronic wound repair but suffer from limitations including external electric power, low activity, and competitive multienzyme reactions. Given this, we developed microenvironment-responsive Janus GOx-Au@PCH–Pt nanoparticles (NPs) as biofuel cells, integrating cascade enzymatic catalysis and self-powered electrical stimulation. The biofuel cell features hydroxylated polyaniline (PCH) NPs as conductive bridges, Pt nanoclusters as the cathode, and glucose oxidase (GOx)-grafted Au (GOx-Au) as the anode. Under infection (acidic pH), conductive PCH shuttles electrons to generate microcurrent that accelerates enzyme catalysis on both the Au anode (GOx) and Pt cathode (peroxidase, POD). The enhanced GOx-POD cascade strengthens ·OH generation, and the self-powered electric field enhances ·OH diffusion across phospholipid bilayers, achieving significant bacterial killing and biofilm dispersion. During tissue repair, neutral/alkaline conditions switch Pt nanozyme from POD to catalase (CAT) and transform PCH into a benzoquinone structure as the electron acceptor. Reversed electron flow boosts the GOx-CAT cascade catalysis on the electrodes, accelerating glucose consumption, suppressing advanced glycation end product formation, and alleviating oxidative stress, while electrical stimulation reduces hypoxia-inducible factor-1α expressions. This synergistic effect promotes collagen deposition and orderly arrangement and normalizes microenvironment with oxygen-generating, hypoglycemic, anti-inflammatory, and macrophage phenotype-shifted features, thereby accelerating wound healing. This designed nanoscale biofuel cells realize adaptive microcurrent modulation and spatiotemporal cascade catalysis, offering a minimally invasive paradigm for infected diabetic wound therapy.
n9c2dfde0cb13: Many soft actuators have been developed to achieve bending deformation under external stimuli through asymmetric structures or nonuniform material distributions. However, most existing actuators can only produce bending in a single direction, and developing soft actuators with deformation reversal capability remains a challenge. To address this issue, this study proposes an MXene-PS/MXene bilayer soft actuator, which is fabricated by sequential vacuum-assisted filtration, resulting in a loose MXene-PS top layer and a dense MXene bottom layer. The MXene-PS layer features a high water absorption/desorption rate but low capacity, while the MXene layer exhibits a low rate but high capacity. This complementary kinetic-capacity coupling mechanism, termed the time-sequence difference of asymmetric water absorption kinetics, enables the actuator to achieve reversible deformation reversal under NIR light and humidity stimuli. Furthermore, simply by changing the placement orientation of the actuator, two distinct self-sustained oscillation behaviors can be obtained in a humidity gradient environment, namely, periodic motion toward or away from the water surface. Leveraging this deformation reversal capability, we demonstrate two proof-of-concept applications: a biomimetic flower and a self-sustained motion sailboat. This work introduces a deformation mode and actuation principle for MXene-based soft actuators and further broadens their application prospects in biomimetic devices and soft robotics.
n0990c8181550: Superconducting topological materials with coexisted superconductivities and topological boundary states are promising platforms for realizing intrinsic topological superconductivity. In this work, the superconducting type-II Dirac semimetal PdTe2 is shown to exhibit clear periodic critical current oscillations in perpendicular magnetic fields due to the fluxoid quantization, indicating the existence of edge superconductivity in PdTe2. Furthermore, a comparative study of the different superconducting properties of the bulk and edge of PdTe2 provides direct evidence for this edge superconductivity. More importantly, by a careful analysis of the flux penetration area, the nontrivial character of the edge superconductivity is revealed, i.e., the edge superconductivity appears not only at the physical boundary of the flake, but also at the interior interface between superconducting and normal regions of PdTe2. The emergence of nontrivial edge superconductivity, indicative of the putative bulk topological superconductivity, not only reveals the great potential of PdTe2 but also provides an experimental avenue for exploring intrinsic topological superconductivity by leveraging bulk-boundary correspondence.
na780e6e8f8fc: Pathological cytokine networks underlie inflammatory injury and tumor-associated immunosuppression, yet most cytokine-targeted therapies rely on molecularly fixed, pathway-specific antagonists. We present a receptor-modular nanomaterial strategy for constructing modular cytokine nanocaptors (MCNs) whose sequestration profiles can be reconfigured by exchanging receptor modules. Cytokine receptor ectodomains are engineered as independently producible serum albumin fusion proteins and coassembled with poly(L-lactic acid) (PLLA) into compositionally defined nanoparticles. This architecture decouples cytokine-binding specificity from nanoparticle structure, enabling high-density codisplay of multiple receptor modules on single particles. Representative MCNs simultaneously sequester IL-6, TNF-α, and IFN-γ and suppress cytokine-driven inflammatory signaling more effectively than matched soluble receptor mixtures. By altering module composition while preserving the same assembly framework, MCNs can be redirected from sequestering pro-inflammatory cytokines in sepsis, acute lung injury, and fulminant hepatitis to depleting immunosuppressive mediators in tumors. These results establish receptor-modular nanocaptors as programmable materials for disease-tailored cytokine sequestration and immune-microenvironment reconfiguration.
n5ca51631d556: Existing hardware implementations of Gaussian random number generators (RNGs) rely on large arrays of binary devices, resulting in substantial hardware footprints or sampling-time overheads. Here, we present a racetrack memory-based random number generator (RTM-RNG) that directly generates analog Gaussian random number streams from a single domain-wall-based nanoscale racetrack. A geometrically engineered racetrack tip creates a localized current-density gradient, enabling field-free stochastic domain-wall nucleation driven by nanosecond current pulses. The domain-wall nucleation probability is continuously tunable via an electrically generated Oersted field or an external magnetic field, providing direct control over the mean of the output distribution. We demonstrate more than 256 distinguishable states from a single nanoscopic RTM-RNG device, thus making a Gaussian RNG with more than 8-bit resolution possible. Compared with conventional binary random bitstreams, the RTM-RNG achieves high-quality Gaussian distributions up to 83 times faster.
nc566a3c7f91e: We demonstrate a pull-middle architecture for standard ternary inverters (STIs) operating at 77 K, enabled by the cointegration of a ZnO–Te antiambipolar switch (AAS) and vertically stacked ZnO/Te complementary field-effect transistors (CFETs) using a BEOL-compatible low-temperature process (≤150 °C). Operation at 77 K not only isolates the intrinsic pull-middle switching mechanism by suppressing thermally activated off-currents but also establishes the architecture’s immediate viability for extreme-environment computing, such as radiation-hardened space data centers and cryogenic aerospace systems. In this architecture, the ZnO–Te AAS acts as an independent pull-middle device connected to an explicit Vdd/2 node, while the ZnO and Te FETs in the CFET serve as the pull-down and pull-up devices, respectively. Unlike conventional ternary logic schemes governed by precise pull-up/pull-down current matching, by explicitly clamping the intermediate state, this architecture structurally prevents variation-induced voltage shifts and suppresses static power dissipation. Consequently, the proposed STI exhibits a narrow middle-state voltage distribution across 25 cells and achieves an I/O swing ratio of 1, with cascaded operation without level-restoring circuitry supported by measurement-calibrated circuit simulations. Ultimately, this vertically integrated ZnO/Te STI offers a compact and variation-tolerant platform for cryogenic logic, while presenting a material-optimization pathway toward room-temperature multivalued systems.
nc5fef1ea1918: Layered oxide cathodes are among the most promising candidates for sodium‐ion batteries (SIBs), offering high capacity, versatile structures, and a compelling cost outlook. However, their journey from laboratory research to widespread commercial use is hampered by a complex set of scientific and engineering challenges. This review provides a comprehensive, cross‐disciplinary analysis of this journey, connecting material design with scalable manufacturing and real‐world market viability. We first establish a foundation by examining the structural polymorphism, degradation mechanisms, and rational element selection that govern cathode performance. The discussion then transitions to industrial production, critically evaluating scalable synthesis methods like coprecipitation, spray drying, and solid‐state reactions, with a focus on reproducibility, cost, and key scaling challenges. Moving to cell‐level integration, we address full‐cell design considerations—including hard carbon anode compatibility, pre‐sodiation strategies, and cell formatting—alongside critical failure modes such as gas generation and thermal runaway. Finally, we situate these technological advances within the broader commercial landscape, analyzing cost structures, emerging application niches, and the evolving policy environment. By synthesizing insights across the entire value chain, this work aims to serve as a strategic guide for researchers and industry professionals working to translate layered oxide cathodes from promising materials into practical, sustainable energy storage solutions.
n19cf28423a85: Fluorinated solvents, salts, and binders are widely used in modern rechargeable batteries. High durability and superior high‐rate ability are often attributed to fluorine‐rich interphases or fluorine‐tuned solvation structures. To date, fluorine‐free battery development is still nascent, with the interphases and structure‐property‐performance relationship thereby remaining poorly understood. Here, we investigate the impact of anion substituents in Na‐ion salts on electrolyte ion transport properties and interphase compositions on Na‐ion anodes. A fluorine‐free sodium tetraphenylborate‐diglyme electrolyte can cycle hard carbon anode over 2000 cycles at 1C with a capacity retention exceeding 98%. Sodium metal anode exhibits stripping‐plating efficiencies of 99.93% over 1000 cycles at 0.5 mA/cm2 and 0.5 mAh/cm2. The steric effect of the bulky phenyl substituent leads to negligible ion pairing and good ionic conductivity, supporting high‐rate performance of Na‐ion electrodes. We demonstrate that a transition‐metal(TM)‐free and fluorine‐free battery as proof of concept, in a perylene‐3,4,9,10‐tetracarboxylic acid diimide (PTCDI)||hard carbon full cell configuration, delivers stable cycling with a ∼85% capacity retention at 1C after 500 cycles and good fast‐charging capability reaching 80% specific energy in less than 4 min. These results show that it is possible to design TM‐free and fluorine‐free sodium ion batteries without an anion‐rich solvation structure or fluorine‐based interphases.
nb5af580b7b13: We report a novel electrolyte that exhibits high reductive stability in the presence of Na metal and enables highly reversible behavior of an in situ formed sodium metal anode. The resulting anode‐less cell achieves 1000 cycles with high‐capacity retention owing to the unique chemistry of the solid‐electrolyte interphase and chemical stability of the carborane. Abstract For anode‐free sodium batteries to achieve practical consideration, highly reversible chemistries require exceptional ≥99.95% coulombic efficiencies that maintain over prolonged cycling periods. To do so, consumption of this severely limited sodium inventory must be restricted while metal nucleation processes that comprise the in situ formed metal anode are improved. Herein, we describe a fluorine‐free carborane electrolyte that satisfies these criteria by emphasizing reductive stability and weakly coordinating anion behavior as design principles. We find this approach promotes the development of a thin, robust SEI chemistry rich in both organic speciation and boron. The electrolyte described herein exhibits ideal metal nucleation behavior on one‐micron thin carbonaceous current collector surfaces and achieves a metal deposition/stripping efficiency near parity for 400 cycles. This novel anode chemistry is introduced to anode‐free full cell configurations where 87% of the initial discharge capacity is retained after 1000 cycles at 2.0 C. Post‐test characterization of deep‐cycled anode‐free cells reveals suppressed capacity fade in these systems is attributed to the chemical stability of the carborane anion.
n5da38a74b526: With sodium‐ion batteries (SIBs) entering the energy market, optimizing their performance has become a key research focus. At the electrode level, the parameters selected during their manufacturing process influence their electrodes microstructure and, consequently, the electrochemical performance. Here, we address different manufacturing conditions of hard carbon (HC) negative electrodes by varying the solid content in the slurry (35 and 40 % SC) and the calendering degree applied to the electrodes (uncalendered and 30 % calendered). The 3D microstructure of each sample is acquired using a focused ion beam (FIB) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) technique, from which the real shape of HC particles is extracted and used to generate input microstructures for a discrete element method (DEM) calendering model designed to address the mechanical electrode behavior and its effects on current collector deformation. Also, the 3D electrode microstructures are used in a finite element method (FEM) model to obtain the electrochemical performance for C‐rates ranging from C/50 to C/2, and to compare these results with experimental ones. Furthermore, the DEM predicted microstructures are also injected into the FEM model to validate the electrochemical performance and compare it with the performance of microstructures reconstructed with FIB‐SEM. We demonstrate a novel approach combining experimentation and advanced mesoscopic modeling, to address how manufacturing parameters influence the performance of HC electrodes, providing an important guideline for optimizing their production for SIB applications.
n09a16a61d481: Electrocatalytic carbon dioxide (CO2) reduction offers a promising pathway for carbon utilization but is severely hindered by the aggressive hydrogen evolution reaction and the structural instability of main‐group metal catalysts in strong acidic solution. Herein, we report the precise anchoring of atomically dispersed In3+ onto the inorganic nodes of MOF‐808, achieving an extraordinarily high loading of 21.8 wt%. The rigid framework of MOF‐808 has abundant open metal sites that securely coordinate with In3+, while its well‐defined 1.8 nm pores ensure rapid mass transport during electrocatalysis. Mechanistic studies reveal that intense electronic coupling of In3+ with the Zr6‐oxo clusters efficiently improves the local electronic structure of the isolated In3+ sites. Consequently, the high In3+ density delivers exceptional performance for selective CO2 reduction to formic acid in acidic electrolyte, achieving an outstanding Faradaic efficiency of 97.1% at −1.2 V vs. RHE. More importantly, the robust spatial confinement for the anchored In3+ within the framework efficiently prevents their chemical leaching and reductive migration, enabling an outstanding long‐term stability of 216 h. This study demonstrates an effective strategy for constructing highly stable and atomically dispersed In3+ catalysts for electrochemical applications in acidic media.
ne0ca90d9baa4: O3‐type layered cathodes for sodium‐ion batteries (NIBs) are promising cathodes, yet they are limited by irreversible phase transitions at high voltages, structural strain, and sluggish Na+ transport, which compromise their cycling and rate performance. Here, a particle engineering strategy using boron oxide to simultaneously stabilize lattice framework, and regulate the crystal facet exposure is proposed. Boron oxide acts as a dual‐function additive, serving as both a flux that governs anisotropic crystal growth and a dopant that reinforces the metal–oxygen network through strong B─O bonding. This dual role drives the formation of submicron hexagonal platelets with a dominant (003) facet orientation and an enlarged Na‐layer spacing, resulting in fast in‐plane Na⁺ diffusion and exceptional structural integrity. Contrary to the conventional view that (003) planes are electrochemically inactive, controlled exposure of these facets suppresses interfacial degradation while maintaining high‐rate kinetics. The optimized boron‐modified cathode achieves excellent cycling stability, with 82.6% capacity retention after 400 cycles at 2C in full cells, together with superior high‐rate performance (92.0 mAh g−1 at 10C). This work illustrates facet engineering via boron modification as an effective and scalable route to reconcile the long‐standing durability–power trade‐off in O3‐type sodium layered oxides.
n16d7e629e461: Although Na‐ and K‐ion batteries are emerging as cost‐effective and sustainable alternatives to Li‐ion batteries (LIBs) for large‐scale energy storage, their distinct physicochemical characteristics present unique challenges in achieving long‐term stability and high electrochemical performance. Among the various performance‐limiting factors, the electrode–electrolyte interphase, including the solid‐electrolyte interphase (SEI) and the cathode–electrolyte interphase (CEI), plays a crucial, yet still insufficiently understood, role in determining battery performances. From this perspective, this review offers critical insights into the interphase characteristics, with a special focus on not only clarifying the comparative characteristics of interphases across alkali‐ion battery systems, but also addressing several key issues often overlooked or misunderstood even in LIB research, including: (i) the dynamic and metastable nature of SEI and CEI, (ii) the limitations of fluorine‐rich CEI, (iii) the critical role of binders for interphase optimization, (iv) the overgeneralization of CEI functionality and formation mechanisms, and (v) the impact of interphase stability and passivation on self‐discharge. In doing so, this review emphasizes the pivotal role of interphase design in electrochemical performance, attempts to redefine the so‐called ideal interphases, and highlights the need for a clear and accurate understanding of the fundamental nature and functionalities of the interphases, beyond the conventional definitions, in alkali metal‐ion battery systems.
ned1800c71587: Studies into the relationship between the volume ratio and the solvation structure produces a TMSPi‐based customized solvation structure that allows the electrolyte of a Na‐metal battery to exhibit enhanced flame‐retardant properties and a superior stability at the electrode–electrolyte interface. This study presents a simple and practical method for electrolyte modification. Abstract Owing to the low cost and high abundance of sodium (Na), significant advancements are made in the field of Na‐based batteries, which are possible through the incorporation of lithium‐ion‐inspired electrodes with different electrolyte chemistries. However, the conventional carbonate electrolytes employed in such systems are flammable, thermally unstable, and prone to severe interfacial side reactions that compromise safety and shorten the overall battery cycle life. This study introduces a flame‐retardant cosolvent strategy, wherein trimethylsilyl phosphite (TMSPi) and nonafluorohexyltrimethoxysilane (NFTOS) are blended into a propylene carbonate (PC)‐based commercial electrolyte, yielding an novel electrolyte system (PCTN) with a tailor‐designed solvation structure. This PCTN electrolyte is found to self‐extinguish upon ignition, in addition to generating a robust NaSiOx/NaF solid electrolyte interphase and a NaPOxFy‐dominated cathode electrolyte interphase. Consequently, the Na|NaNi0.4Fe0.2Mn0.4O2 cell incorporating PCTN retained 90.3% of its initial capacity after 450 cycles at 1 C, outperforming commercial electrolytes. Even at a high operation temperature of 70 °C, a capacity retention of 93.2% is achieved after 100 cycles using PCTN (c.f., 79.9% for a commercial electrolyte). Overall, this work demonstrates a facile, production‐compatible electrolyte design that synchronously enhances the stability of the electrode–electrolyte interface, offering a potential system for incorporation into next‐generation high‐performance Na metal batteries.
n696878f84998: Gas evolution behaviors of sodium layered oxide cathodes with varying compositions, cutoff voltages, dopants, and particle sizes/morphologies have been systematically investigated by online electrochemical mass spectrometry. The fundamental outgassing mechanisms of sodium‐based cathodes compared to lithium‐based cathodes have been elucidated. Multi‐phase side reaction products—both soluble and solid—have been quantified by nuclear magnetic resonance and X‐ray photoelectron spectroscopies, respectively. Abstract Sodium‐ion batteries (SIBs) are attractive for the low cost and abundance of sodium. Yet, gas evolution—a critical challenge in SIBs—remains underexplored. Here, online electrochemical mass spectrometry is used to probe gas evolution in layered oxide cathodes with various compositions, cutoff voltages, dopants, and particle morphologies. Compared to LiNiO2 (LNO), NaNiO2 releases more gas, even at lower states of charge, due to the higher covalency of Ni─O bond caused by the more ionic Na─O bond through the inductive effect. Among Co, Mn, Al, and Mg, Mn and Mg doping suppress gas release most effectively by enhancing the metal‐oxygen bond strength. NaNi1/3Fe1/3Mn1/3O2 (NFM) cathodes synthesized via coprecipitation (CP‐NFM) and solid‐state routes exhibit distinct particle morphologies; CP‐NFM exhibits more gas evolution, yet secondary particle morphology helps reduce it through differential cathode‐electrolyte reactivity between inner and outer primary particles. Among Li, Ti, Mg, and Cu doping in NFM, Li has the largest effect, reducing gas levels comparable to LNO. Nuclear magnetic resonance and X‐ray photoelectron spectroscopies reveal that electrolyte solvent decomposition mainly produces organic‐rich cathode‐electrolyte interphase (CEI) rather than soluble species. NaPF6 salt further exacerbates cathode‐electrolyte reactions, forming surface Na2O species. The findings provide actionable guidance for designing safer, durable SIBs.
n5f2fc1308c05: Sodium–sulfur (Na–S) all‐solid‐state batteries (ASSBs) hold great promise for large‐scale energy storage owing to their low cost and high energy density, but face persistent interfacial challenges. This review highlights recent advances in electrode/electrolyte design, interfacial engineering, and outlines future research directions toward practical Na–S ASSBs. Abstract The increasing global energy demand has accelerated the development of cost‐effective energy storage technologies. Among various alternatives to conventional lithium‐ion batteries, sodium‐sulfur (Na–S) all‐solid‐state batteries (ASSBs) have emerged as a promising solution due to the abundance and low cost of sodium and sulfur. While traditional high‐temperature Na–S batteries offer high energy densities, their elevated operational temperatures (> 300 °C) pose significant safety and cost challenges. To mitigate these issues, low‐temperature (LT) Na–S ASSBs (operating below 80 °C) have gained attention for their improved safety, reduced maintenance costs, and high theoretical capacity. However, they still face critical obstacles such as poor electrode–electrolyte contact and sluggish interfacial kinetics. This review focuses on recent advancements in LT Na–S battery technology, particularly those employing solid‐state electrolytes. A comprehensive discussion is provided on the critical design principles for cathodes, anodes, and electrolytes, highlighting the progress, challenges, and opportunities associated with each component. Finally, the perspective on future research directions necessary to realize practical, high‐performance LT Na–S ASSBs for large‐scale energy storage applications is presented.
nf8b3692ef799: This study employs an iron‐valence‐controlled strategy to tailor the local structure of Na4Fe3(PO4)2P2O7. The optimized Na4.024Fe2.921(PO4)2P2O7 achieves an optimal balance in the ordering and proportion of inert Na2 site, enabling superior Na+ kinetics and stability (capacity retention of 90.7% after 10,000 cycles). The sodium‐ion full cells demonstrate exceptional wide‐temperature performance from −40 to 45 °C. Abstract Iron‐based mixed‐phosphate Na4Fe3(PO4)2P2O7 (NFPP) is a representative cathode for sodium‐ion batteries owing to its low cost and environmental compatibility. The behavior of sodium ions in NFPP is governed by four crystallographically distinguishable sodium sites, yet the underlying mechanism for occupation sites and diffusion kinetics remains not fully understood. Herein, a scalable synthesis strategy for NFPP materials with tunable local structures is proposed by controlling the iron valence during preparation. The nonstoichiometric Na4.024Fe2.921(PO4)2P2O7 strikes an optimal balance between the ordering and proportion of inert sodium ions. These ordered inert sodium ions act as structural pillars, providing markedly enhanced stability compared to disordered counterparts. The optimized sodium environment leads to a synergistic enhancement of both thermal stability and sodium ionic kinetics. The cathode delivers a remarkable rate performance and cycling stability (90.7% capacity retention after 10,000 cycles). This exceptional stability is corroborated by a small lattice volume variation of 4.18% upon desodiation. Moreover, cylindrical full cells assembled with kilogram‐scale Na4.024Fe2.921(PO4)2P2O7 cathode and a hard carbon anode demonstrate excellent performance across a wide temperature range from −40 to 45 °C. This work establishes the critical interplay between local environment and electrochemical properties, offering valuable insights for the design of advanced cathode materials.
n1164a3816bd4: Sodium layered oxides Na x MO2 (x ≤ 1 and M = transition metal ions) have gained significant interest as sodium-ion battery (NIB) cathodes owing to their high operating voltages and potential for higher energy density compared with polyanion and Prussian blue–type cathodes. However, their practical applications are often hindered by the irreversible structural transitions leading to capacity fading during cycling. The nature and substitution of transition metal ions define the material properties and electrochemical performance. In this study, through comprehensive electrochemical characterization combined with multi-scale structural and spectroscopical analyses, we demonstrate the synergistic impacts of Lithium and Titanium doping, which not only increases overall capacity by boosting cation and anion cooperative redox contributions but also improves the rate capability and cycling stability. Specifically, Li+ doping enhances the available sodium inventory for extraction, while Ti4 + disrupts Na+/vacancy ordering at lower voltages (< 4 V) and mitigates the detrimental P2→OP4/O2 phase transition during cycling. The combined effect of Lithium and Titanium doping promotes more charge localization on Oxygen, which activates reversible lattice oxygen redox reactions at elevated voltages, contributing additional capacity beyond conventional cationic redox. This work provides crucial insights into the design of high-performance, high-capacity P2-type layered cathode materials for sodium-ion batteries.
n58ca314e0400: The design of composite cathodes for all‐solid‐state sodium batteries must address three critical challenges—interfacial side reactions, interfacial delamination, and highly tortuous transport pathways. This work outlines structural and interfacial strategies to optimize ion transport and mechanical stability, enabling durable, and high‐performance solid‐state sodium battery systems. Abstract All‐solid‐state sodium‐ion batteries (ASSSBs) are regarded as highly promising candidates for large‐scale energy storage systems owing to their expected lower cost and enhanced safety. In recent years, the advent of novel fast ion‐conducting solid electrolytes (SEs) has further accelerated the rapid development of this field. Nevertheless, several critical challenges remain, preventing the performance of ASSSBs from surpassing that of their liquid‐electrolyte counterparts. Among these, a key obstacle lies in the design of cathode systems that ensure optimal compatibility between the SE and the cathode active material (CAM). This review focuses on the essential properties and persistent challenges of CAM in ASSSBs employing inorganic SEs and highlights the current strategies developed to address these issues. Particular attention is given to the design considerations at the cathode, particle, and interface levels, including aspects related to the microstructure, mechanical integrity, and (electro)chemical interactions with the SE. Finally, the review outlines future directions and design principles for the development of next‐generation cathode materials in ASSSBs.
n2f053d95249c: Na‐ion batteries (SIBs) have emerged as a cost‐effective and scalable energy storage solution, particularly suited for grid‐level applications and affordable electric mobility. As the demand for rapid energy delivery grows, enabling fast‐charge/discharge capability in SIBs has become increasingly critical. However, the sluggish Na+ transport kinetics and interfacial instability under fast‐charge/discharge conditions remain significant bottlenecks toward commercialization. This review presents a comprehensive analysis of degradation mechanisms and technical breakthroughs for enabling fast‐charge/discharge SIBs, structured across three scales: electrode material, interface, and system.
